content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Construct a table of values for a linear equation
Plot points from a table of values on a coordinate grid
Recognise and plot horizontal and vertical lines
Understand the link between an equation and its graph
Linear graphs appear throughout science, engineering, and everyday life. When a taxi charges a fixed fee plus a rate per mile, the cost increases

with distance — and plotting this relationship produces a straight line. Understanding how to plot linear graphs from their equations is a fundamental skill that underpins all graphical work in mathematics.

Without plotting, explain how you know the lines $y = 4x + 1$ and $y = 4x - 3$ are parallel.
$y = 3$: horizontal line through $(0, 3)$. $y = -1$: horizontal line through $(0, -1)$. $x = 2$: vertical line through $(2, 0)$. $x = -3$: vertical line through $(-3, 0)$.
Table: $(-3,-3)$, $(-2,-2)$, $\ldots$, $(3,3)$. A straight line through the origin at 45°.
Rearrange: already in form. Use multiples of 3 for easy values: $(-6, -1)$, $(-3, 0)$, $(0, 1)$, $(3, 2)$, $(6, 3)$.
Both lines have the same coefficient of $x$ (gradient $= 4$), so they are parallel. They are simply shifted vertically: one crosses the $y$-axis at $1$ and the other at $-3$.
